title: Felix and the Undertow
premise: Ada Okonkwo, a night librarian who has spent years perfecting the art of being overlooked, is asked by Mr. Felix Adeyemi—the last fluent speaker of Ọ̀rọ̀ Ilẹ̀, a dying Nigerian language—to become his final student. As their nightly lessons unfold, Ada discovers old photographs linking Felix to her late mother, whom she has long resented for abandoning her, and realizes the language itself carries her family's buried history. When Felix's health fails and the city's redevelopment threatens to demolish his home and archive, Ada must choose between retreating into her invisibility or publicly fighting to preserve what remains. She records Felix's last words, testifies at the demolition hearing in a language she can now speak, and finally forgives her mother—understanding that belonging was never something she lost, but something she must carry forward.
about_author: Zephyrine Eastwick is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing endangered-language recordings before turning to fiction. They write about quiet people and loud histories from a coastal town where the fog does most of the talking.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. We meet Ada during a sleepless night shift in a city that never darkens, watching her deflect every human connection with practiced ease. An elderly man, Felix Adeyemi, arrives asking for help finding 'a student'—and leaves a card with a single word in an alphabet Ada doesn't recognize. The emotional beat: loneliness revealed as armor, and the first crack in it.

chapters.title: Lessons in a Dying Tongue
chapters.summary: Alternating Ada and Felix POVs. Ada begins secret lessons in Felix's cluttered house; the language resists her, and so does intimacy. Among his belongings she finds photographs of a young woman who looks unmistakably like her mother. The beat: wonder shadowed by dread, as learning to speak becomes learning to look.

chapters.title: What the Photographs Kept
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, with Felix's recorded voice threading through. Confronted, Felix reveals he loved Ada's mother, who was his first student before she fled the language—and him—to build a new life. Demolition notices arrive; Felix collapses mid-lesson. The climax: rage, grief, and the choice between walking away or standing in the wreckage of two betrayals.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker Speaks
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. In Felix's final weeks, Ada records his voice and memorizes his stories, then stands before the demolition board and speaks for him—in Ọ̀rọ̀ Ilẹ̀, imperfect but unashamed. She wins a reprieve for the archive, buries her resentment of her mother beside Felix's grave, and opens the library's doors wider than her smile ever could. The beat: belonging, finally chosen.
